To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the Griffith criterion breaks down at small scales; and (ii) optimal adhesion can occur at small scales, provided the characteristic size of the adhesion device is sufficiently small.

(i) the Griffith theory of fracture is not valid for small scale systems, (ii) small scale systems fail at their theoretical strengths, (iii) adhesion strength can be increased by reducing the size of contact area, (iv) adhesion strength is robust to the presence of surface defects, (v) optimal adhesion can also be achieved by optimizing the shape of adhesion elements, but this is not robust to surface defects.
materials with nanoscale substructure are inherently flaw-tolerant and can fail at their theoretical limit.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the fundamental understanding of the mechanical properties of nanomaterials and nanostructures, with a focus on failure and adhesion phenomena.
the size dependence of fracture and adhesion at the nanoscale.
understanding the mechanics of nanoscale structures and the role of length scale on the mechanical properties and performance of materials.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
at small scales, the classical mechanisms of failure of materials and adhesion may no longer hold, and new mechanisms may be needed to explain the failure of nanoscale structures and adhesion.
the size of materials and adhesion systems has a profound effect on their failure and adhesion properties.
nanoscale materials can be flaw tolerant, and can achieve optimal adhesion strength.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
at the nanoscale, both failure and adhesion become size-dependent and can be optimized by reducing the characteristic dimensions of the materials.
the size of materials and the shape of the surfaces of materials play a crucial role in the mechanical behaviour of small-scale materials.
nanoscale systems can be designed to be either robust or optimal, but not both.
The main takeaway from our work is that
at the nanoscale, materials and devices can be designed with optimal properties that are robust against flaws, defects and roughness.

at nanoscale, failure and deformation mechanisms are drastically different from those observed at macroscale, and that this size-dependent transition in failure mechanisms can be exploited in the design of nanostructured materials.

at small scales, classical continuum mechanics fails to provide a complete understanding of failure mechanisms, and that atomistic simulations may provide a more complete understanding of the failure mechanisms of nanoscale systems.
